content.title: About
content.content: Canned bluberries are ripe berries harvested at peak ripeness, cleaned and packed in glass or metal jars with a light syrup or their own juice. The berries retain their sweet‑tart flavor, bright color, and most of their nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Bluberries are considered a “super‑fruit” because of their high antioxidant content, especially anthocyanins.
Canning allows the berries to be stored for up to a year without losing flavor or most vitamins.
In the United States canned bluberries are commonly used in pies, desserts, and sauces.
Bluberries grow in northern regions of North America, Europe and Asia.
The syrup used in cans usually contains a small amount of sugar, but sugar‑free versions are available.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins help protect cells from oxidative stress and support eye health.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Flavonoids improve circulation and may lower LDL cholesterol.

items.title: Vitamin C source
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber aids digestion and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Bluberries provide potassium, magnesium and iron, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The syrup can increase the product’s calorie count; choose a no‑added‑sugar version if you monitor blood sugar.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to bluberries.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some brands add preservatives; check the label if you are sensitive.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canned bluberries can be eaten straight from the jar, added to yogurt, oatmeal, smoothies, baked goods, desserts, or used as a topping for pancakes and waffles. You may drain the syrup and rinse the berries if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if mold or off‑odors appear.

chicken-thigh-fried-coated-skin-coating-.title: Chicken thigh, fried, coated, skin/coating eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Chicken thigh, deep‑fried in a crispy coating, is ready to eat. Both the skin and the breading are edible, giving the dish a rich flavor and texture. The product falls under the pre‑cooked meat category (code 847).

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Frying at high temperature creates a golden crust that locks in juices.
Thigh meat contains more fat than breast, making it juicier after frying.
The coating is usually made from wheat flour, spices, and sometimes breadcrumbs, adding aroma and crunch.
Such dishes are classic staples of fast‑food and street cuisine worldwide.
When stored properly, the ready‑to‑eat product can last several days in the fridge.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Chicken thigh provides high‑quality animal protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: The meat contains niacin (B3) and pyridoxine (B6), which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from the meat helps maintain normal hemoglobin levels.

items.title: Moderate fat content
items.content: The fat adds flavor and aids absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potassium supports fluid balance and heart function.

items.title: High in fat and calories
items.content: Fried meat can contribute to weight gain if consumed in excess.

items.title: Sodium in the coating
items.content: Salt added to the breading raises sodium intake, which may be undesirable for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: If the coating contains wheat flour, people with celiac disease should choose a gluten‑free version.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage can allow pathogens such as Salmonella to grow.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to eat straight from the package after reheating. It can be served as a main dish, in burgers, salads, with sauces, or as a snack. Adding fresh vegetables or a squeeze of lemon balances the richness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at 0–4 °C in the original packaging or an airtight container. Once opened, consume within 3–5 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C, though coating quality may decline.

ravioli-ns-as-to-filling-with-cream-sauc.title: Ravioli with NS filling and cream sauce

content.title: About
content.content: Ravioli are small pasta parcels filled with an NS (natural cheese, spinach) mixture and served with a smooth cream sauce. The dough is made from durum wheat, while the filling gives the dish a mild, slightly cheesy flavor with a hint of freshness.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ravioli originated in Italy and have been made for over a thousand years.
The combination of NS filling and cream sauce is popular in modern fusion cuisine, merging Italian pasta with Northern European dairy flavors.
Ravioli can be prepared fresh or frozen for later use.
Cream sauce is often made from heavy cream, butter, and a touch of Parmesan, giving it a velvety texture.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Durum wheat dough and the cheese component of the filling provide a good amount of both plant and dairy protein.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D
items.content: The cream sauce and cheese contribute notable calcium levels, supporting bone health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Durum wheat and cheese contain vitamins B1, B2, and B6, which aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: If spinach is added to the filling, the fiber content increases, benefiting digestion.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Durum wheat has a lower glycemic index than soft wheat, helping to moderate blood sugar spikes.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The cream sauce and cheese may trigger allergic reactions in individuals with lactose intolerance or milk protein allergy.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce and cheese make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑managed diets.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Durum wheat dough contains gluten, so the product is unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Cream sauces often contain salt; those monitoring sodium intake should choose a low‑salt version.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Boil ravioli in salted water for 3‑5 minutes until al dente, then drizzle with hot cream sauce. Serve as a main dish or pair with a green salad, grated Parmesan, or fresh herbs.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh ravioli keep in the refrigerator for up to 2 days in an airtight container. Frozen ravioli last up to 3 months in the freezer. Store the cream sauce separately, refrigerated for up to 5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Pork stew with pasta is a hearty dish where tender pieces of pork are slowly cooked in a flavorful sauce together with pasta. The combination of savory meat, creamy sauce texture and al dente pasta makes it a favorite for family lunches and dinners.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Slow cooking makes pork especially tender and allows it to absorb the sauce flavors.
Short‑shaped pasta such as penne or farfalle is traditionally used so the sauce clings better.
Pork is a rich source of vitamin B12, important for the nervous system.
In many regions the dish is finished with grated Parmesan and fresh herbs.
The stew can be prepared in a slow cooker, saving time while preserving aroma.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork provides complete protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Iron from pork helps maintain hemoglobin levels and prevents anemia.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dish supplies vitamins B1, B6 and B12, which support energy metabolism.

items.title: Carbohydrates from pasta
items.content: Pasta offers a quick source of energy and a modest amount of fiber.

items.title: Zinc content
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Fatty cuts of pork can be calorie‑dense; choose lean cuts or trim excess fat.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Sauces and seasonings often contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Wheat pasta contains gluten, making the dish unsuitable for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Thorough cooking required
items.content: Pork must be fully cooked to avoid food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Sear pork cubes until golden, then add onion, carrot and tomato sauce. Simmer on low heat for 1–1.5 hours, adding pasta 15 minutes before the end. Add broth or water as needed to keep the sauce from drying out.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the stew to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. When frozen, it keeps for up to 2 months; thaw in the fridge before reheating.

turkey-and-ham-sandwich-or-sub-with-chee.title: Turkey and Ham Sandwich or Sub with Cheese

content.title: About
content.content: The turkey and ham sandwich with cheese is a classic quick‑lunch option offered by the restaurant founded in 1867. Tender turkey, savory ham and melted cheese are layered between a soft roll or a long sub bun, often complemented by fresh vegetables and a sauce.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish originated in the United States in the early 20th century as a convenient way to use leftover roasted turkey.
A “sub” (or “hoagie”) is typically served on a longer roll, allowing for more filling.
The combination of turkey and ham provides a contrast of mild and salty flavors.
Cheese is usually chosen as a meltable variety so it quickly binds the other ingredients.
Restaurant 1867 is known for using only fresh, preservative‑free ingredients.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Turkey and ham supply high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin rich
items.content: Poultry and ham provide vitamins B6 and B12, supporting nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Melted cheese adds calcium, important for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: When made with whole‑grain bread, the sandwich fits well into low‑carb dietary plans.

items.title: Nutrient‑dense veggies
items.content: Adding lettuce, tomato or cucumber boosts fiber, vitamins and antioxidants.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Ham and processed cheese can be high in salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Preservatives
items.content: Some hams contain nitrites; choose nitrate‑free options if you prefer.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger reactions in individuals allergic to milk proteins.

items.title: Meat quality
items.content: Use fresh turkey and ham without signs of spoilage to avoid foodborne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the roll in half, layer turkey, then ham, and place a slice of cheese on top. Add lettuce, tomato, cucumber and your favorite sauce. Warm in the oven or on a grill if you like the cheese melted.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the assembled sandwich in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Store the separate ingredients (sliced turkey, ham, cheese) wrapped in plastic and use within 3‑4 days.
